A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of constant right-sided
scrotal pain. The pain began several hours prior to presentation and awoke him from sleep. He
is an otherwise healthy boy who states he has never experienced pain like this before. He
denies a history of genital trauma or any sexual activity, and he has not noticed any swelling or
lumps in his groin. He has not had any fevers, chills, urinary frequency, dysuria, hematuria, or
urethral discharge.

A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.

A 12-year-old boy is brought by his parents for a persistent cough that has lasted 3 weeks and is progressively worsening. The illness began with 1 week of runny nose and mild cough that was initially thought to be a cold. The cough then intensified into severe paroxysms of rapid, consecutive coughs followed by a whooping inspiratory sound. He has had several episodes of post-tussive vomiting. He occasionally turns red in the face during coughing fits. Between episodes he appears relatively well. His vaccination records show he received DTaP at 2, 4, and 6 months but missed his preschool and adolescent boosters. Vital signs are normal between episodes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. A nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis returns positive. CBC shows a white blood cell count of 18,000 with 70% lymphocytes.

A 12-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after experiencing a brief nosebleed from his left nostril approximately 30 minutes ago. The bleeding lasted about 5 minutes and stopped with firm pinching of the nose. His mother reports the house has been very dry due to winter heating, and she has noticed him picking his nose frequently. He denies any history of easy bruising, prolonged bleeding from cuts, or prior nosebleeds requiring medical attention. On examination, there is a small dried blood clot visible at the anterior septum of the left nostril. No active bleeding is noted. The remainder of the nasal exam is normal.

A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. He is able to take oral fluids and is instructed on the appropriate oral fluid and electrolyte rehydration.

A 14-year-old boy who swims competitively is brought in by his parent for evaluation of a bump on the bottom of his right foot that has been growing over the past 2 months. It is generally painless but occasionally mildly uncomfortable with direct pressure during walking. He denies any pain at rest or other similar lesions. On examination, there is a single well-circumscribed, rough, raised lesion approximately 8 mm on the plantar surface of the right foot at the base of the third metatarsal. Pinpoint black dots are visible within the lesion. Skin lines are interrupted around the lesion. No surrounding erythema is noted.

A 14-year-old boy with no significant past medical history presents 3 days after developing a red, irritated right eye that spread to the left eye today. He has watery discharge from both eyes and they are stuck shut in the morning. He reports recent upper respiratory symptoms and that several children at his day camp recently had pink eye. He denies significant pain or light sensitivity and does not wear contact lenses. On examination, his pupils are equal and reactive and he has a right-sided, tender preauricular lymph node. Penlight examination does not reveal any corneal opacity

A 15-year-old girl presents with a superficial scrape on her left knee after falling off her skateboard approximately 1 hour ago. She was wearing shorts and fell onto pavement. She cleaned the wound with water at home. She denies hitting her head, loss of consciousness, or any other injuries. Her tetanus immunization is up to date. On examination, there is a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion on the anterior left knee with minor oozing of serous fluid. There is no active arterial bleeding, no embedded foreign material visible, and no involvement of deeper tissue. The surrounding skin is intact. Range of motion of the knee is full and painless.

A 15-year-old girl presents with her mother for evaluation of bumps on her forehead and chin that have been present for the past 3 months. She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. She denies any cystic lesions, scarring, or use of new cosmetics. Menarche was 1 year ago and her cycles are regular. She takes no medications. On examination, there are scattered open and closed comedones on the forehead and chin numbering approximately 15 to 20. A few small inflammatory papules, each less than 5 mm, are noted on the chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring.

Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.

A 16-year-old male competitive swimmer presents with a 4-day history of progressive right ear pain and itching. He has been swimming daily for the past 3 weeks during summer training. The pain worsens when he chews food and when he lies on his right side. He reports a sensation of fullness in the ear and mild hearing reduction. He denies fever, ear discharge, or recent upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is marked tenderness on manipulation of the right tragus and with traction on the right auricle. Otoscopic examination reveals a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. The tympanic membrane is barely visible but appears intact. The left ear examination is normal. There is no periauricular lymphadenopathy, mastoid tenderness, or facial nerve dysfunction.

A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Labs: acetaminophen level 180 mcg/mL (well above treatment line on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 12 hours), AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, INR 1.8, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. N-acetylcysteine infusion is initiated immediately. Psychiatry and social work consultations are placed. Poison control is contacted.

A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.

A 19-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of severe sore throat that has progressively worsened despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin prescribed for pharyngitis. He now reports difficulty swallowing and has been unable to eat solid food for 2 days. He describes a muffled "hot potato" voice and difficulty fully opening his mouth. He has been drooling due to pain with swallowing. He denies respiratory difficulty. Vital signs show temperature 101.4°F, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124/78. On examination, there is trismus with limited mouth opening to approximately 2 cm. Intraoral exam reveals a bulging, erythematous soft palate on the left with displacement of the left tonsil medially and inferiorly. The uvula is deviated to the right. There is tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation is clear and there is no stridor.

He used a new razor and shaved without moisturizing first. He denies any prior skin conditions or allergies. On examination, there is diffuse erythema with multiple small non-follicular papules along the anterior and lateral neck. There is no pustulation, vesiculation, or excoriation. The affected area is slightly warm to touch. No lymphadenopathy or deeper tissue involvement is noted. The remainder of the skin exam is normal.

A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.

He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or testicular trauma. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. There is tenderness and induration localized to the left epididymis posterior to the testis. Prehn sign is positive with relief of pain on elevation of the left testis. The cremasteric reflex is present bilaterally. There is no testicular torsion on clinical assessment. Urinalysis shows 15 to 20 WBC per high-power field. A nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia and gonorrhea is sent.

A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. Her partner reports she has complained of a persistent headache, visual disturbances described as flashing lights, and swelling of her face and hands over the past 2 days. She did not attend her last two prenatal appointments. On examination, she is postictal, moaning, and not following commands. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112, RR 22, BP 182/116, SpO2 94%. Significant periorbital and bilateral upper extremity edema is present. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally with sustained clonus at the ankles. Fetal heart rate monitoring shows persistent late decelerations. Labs: platelets 92,000/mcL, AST 286 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, LDH 680 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 5.2. IV magnesium sulfate is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is planned.

A 25-year-old male military recruit collapses during an outdoor training exercise on a hot, humid day (ambient temperature 102F, humidity 85%). Fellow recruits report he was initially confused and staggering before losing consciousness. He was wearing full gear and had limited water breaks. On examination, he is unresponsive to verbal commands but withdraws from painful stimuli (GCS 8). Vital signs: T 41.1C (106F) via rectal thermometer, HR 148, RR 32, BP 86/52, SpO2 93%. His skin is hot, flushed, and notably dry with absence of sweating (anhidrosis). Pupils are dilated but reactive. He exhibits decorticate posturing intermittently. Labs: sodium 152 mEq/L, potassium 5.8 mEq/L, creatinine 2.6 mg/dL, AST 482 U/L, ALT 326 U/L, CK 12,400 U/L, lactate 7.2 mmol/L, INR 1.6, platelets 98,000/mcL. Aggressive cooling measures are initiated including cold water immersion, ice packs to axillae and groin, and cold IV saline infusion.

A 25-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician after experiencing her fourth episode in the past 6 weeks of sudden-onset palpitations, shortness of breath, chest tightness, diaphoresis, trembling, and an intense fear of dying. The episodes reach peak intensity within minutes and typically last 15 to 30 minutes before gradually subsiding. Between episodes she has developed significant anticipatory anxiety and has begun avoiding crowded places such as shopping malls and public transportation. She has presented to the emergency department twice during episodes, where cardiac workup including ECG, troponin, and chest radiograph were normal. She has no medical history and no family history of cardiac disease. Vital signs today are normal. Physical examination is unremarkable. Thyroid function tests, CBC, and basic metabolic panel are normal. A 24-hour Holter monitor showed sinus tachycardia during one symptomatic episode only.

The pain initially occurred only during long runs but now is present with walking and at rest. She significantly increased her training mileage six weeks ago in preparation for an upcoming marathon. She has a history of irregular menstrual periods and follows a restrictive diet. On examination, there is focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal. A 28-year-old woman presents with a 9-month history of chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and unintentional weight loss of 12 pounds. She reports 3 to 5 loose stools daily and intermittent crampy abdominal pain. She has also noticed increasing fatigue and occasional mouth sores. Her past medical history is unremarkable except for iron deficiency anemia diagnosed 6 months ago that has been poorly responsive to oral iron supplementation. On examination, she appears thin with a BMI of 18.5. She is pale. Abdominal examination reveals mild diffuse tenderness without organomegaly. There are no skin rashes. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL with a low MCV of 72, ferritin 8 ng/mL, and low serum vitamin D at 15 ng/mL. Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody is elevated at 98 units (normal less than 20). Total IgA level is normal.

On examination, there is diffuse erythema of the palmar surface of the left index finger from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint. The skin is intact with no blistering or blanching. The area is tender to light touch and warm. Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds. Sensation and range of motion of the finger are intact.

A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch. Hemoglobin returns at 7.8 g/dL. O-negative blood is ordered and the OR is alerted for emergent laparotomy.

She reports associated fever and chills and feeling generally unwell. A 28-year-old woman with known epilepsy is brought in by ambulance after her roommate witnessed continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes. EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. Her roommate reports she recently missed several doses of medication due to insurance issues. On arrival, she remains in continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Vital signs: T 39.2C, HR 142, RR (irregular, 8-30), BP 168/98, SpO2 88% on non-rebreather mask. She is cyanotic around the lips. Finger-stick glucose is 142 mg/dL. IV lorazepam 4 mg is administered with brief cessation of convulsive activity, but seizures resume within 2 minutes.

month ago, while taking a shower, he noted a hard area in his right testis that felt "like a

physical exams and was never told that a lump was present. Four years ago, he had a scrotal
ultrasound following a brief episode of scrotal discomfort after competing in a bicycle race; the
result of the ultrasound was normal.

A 29-year-old man comes to the office because he has had weight loss, lethargy, and postural
dizziness for the past 2 months. He says his symptoms began just after surgery to repair a
diaphragmatic hernia caused by a stab wound to the chest 6 months ago. He first went to the
emergency department 3 weeks after surgery because of sharp right-sided chest pain. At that
time, CT scan of the chest was obtained to rule out pulmonary embolism, which was suspected
because he was found to have low blood pressure along with his chest pain. No evidence of
pulmonary embolism was noted on CT scan. He was discharged home on an antiemetic and
acetaminophen. Today he says that, since the operation, he has had gradually worsening
lethargy, morning nausea with occasional vomiting, and generalized abdominal pain. He feels
very dizzy when he stands up and has lost 12 kg in the last 2 months.

A 29-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician reporting 8 months of near-constant excessive worry about multiple domains of her life including work performance, finances, health, and her children's safety. She describes an inability to control the worry despite recognizing it is disproportionate. She reports associated restlessness, muscle tension predominantly in her neck and shoulders, difficulty falling asleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating during meetings. She has tried meditation and exercise with only partial benefit. She denies panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive thoughts, or traumatic experiences. She has no prior psychiatric history and takes no medications. She drinks one cup of coffee daily. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals bilateral trapezius muscle tightness but is otherwise unremarkable. Thyroid function tests are within normal limits. GAD-7 score is 16 indicating severe anxiety.

A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Over the past several days, she has noticed redness in both eyes without discharge, a rash on his trunk, swelling of his hands and feet, cracked bleeding lips, and a red bumpy tongue. He has been increasingly irritable and refusing to eat. On examination, the child is febrile, irritable, and difficult to console. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 148, RR 28, BP 86/52. Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection is present. Lips are erythematous with fissures. A prominent strawberry tongue is noted. A diffuse polymorphous maculopapular rash covers the trunk and perineum with early desquamation in the groin. Bilateral hands and feet show indurative edema with erythema. Right anterior cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 2.0 cm is palpable. Labs: WBC 18,600/mcL, ESR 82 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 488,000/mcL, ALT 68 U/L. Echocardiogram reveals dilated left anterior descending coronary artery (z-score 3.2). IVIG and high-dose aspirin are initiated.

A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after a skiing accident in which he sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, which was splinted in the field by ski patrol. He reports that his pain has been escalating dramatically despite receiving IV morphine 10 mg total, which is atypical for the degree of injury. He describes the pain as deep and burning, significantly worse with any passive movement of his right toes. On examination, the right lower leg appears tense and swollen within the splint. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 142/88, SpO2 99%. After splint removal, the anterior compartment of the right leg is firm and exquisitely tender. Pain is markedly worsened with passive extension of the right toes. Sensation is diminished in the first web space (deep peroneal nerve distribution). Dorsalis pedis pulse is still palpable but diminished compared to the left. Compartment pressure measurement reveals 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment (diastolic BP 88, delta pressure 40 mmHg). Orthopedic surgery is consulted for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

The headaches are usually associated with exertion or with straining during bowel movements but sometimes occur without any provocation. She has not been evaluated for these headaches before.

A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. The uterus is firm, tender, and contracted (woody consistency) with no relaxation between contractions. Moderate dark red vaginal bleeding is present. Continuous fetal monitoring reveals a baseline fetal heart rate of 170 bpm with absent variability and repetitive late decelerations. Labs: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 108,000/mcL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL (low), PT 14.8 seconds, D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL. Transfusion is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is called.

A 32-year-old woman presents with a 10-month history of recurrent episodes of abdominal cramping and altered bowel habits. She describes lower abdominal pain that is relieved with defecation, alternating between periods of diarrhea lasting several days and constipation lasting a week. Symptoms worsen during periods of work-related stress. She denies blood in her stool, nocturnal symptoms, fever, or weight loss. Family history is negative for inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears anxious but in no acute distress. Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant with a palpable sigmoid colon on deep palpation. No masses, organomegaly, or guarding. Rectal examination is normal. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and thyroid function tests are within normal limits. Stool calprotectin is negative.

A 32-year-old woman who is 4 months postpartum presents with a 6-week history of pain along the radial (thumb) side of her right wrist. The pain began insidiously and has progressively worsened. She attributes it to the repetitive motions of lifting and holding her infant. The pain is sharp and radiates proximally into the forearm and distally into the thumb. She reports difficulty gripping objects, turning her wrist, and making a fist. She is right-hand dominant. On examination, there is tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid process and the first dorsal compartment. Finkelstein test is markedly positive, reproducing sharp pain along the radial wrist when the thumb is grasped in a fist and the wrist is ulnarly deviated. Grip strength is reduced due to pain. Thumb range of motion is preserved but painful at extremes. Neurovascular examination of the hand is intact. Wrist radiographs are normal.

A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.

He reports significant fatigue and an unintentional 10-pound weight loss over the past month. On examination, he appears cachectic and is in mild respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.4C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 108/68, SpO2 88% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral diffuse crackles. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates with a ground-glass pattern. LDH is markedly elevated at 580 U/L. Induced sputum is sent for silver stain.

A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

A 38-year-old obese woman presents with a 2-day history of worsening right upper quadrant pain that began after eating fried chicken. The pain is constant, radiates to her right scapula, and is associated with nausea and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. She has had intermittent postprandial bloating and epigastric discomfort over the past year that she attributed to indigestion. She denies jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 130/84. On examination, she is moderately uncomfortable. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest during palpation of the RUQ). There is no rebound tenderness, rigidity, or palpable mass. Right upper quadrant ultrasound reveals a distended gallbladder with gallstones, wall thickening to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign. The common bile duct measures 4 mm.

A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

A 45-year-old male farmer is brought in by coworkers after collapsing in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. Coworkers report he initially complained of blurred vision and a headache, then developed profuse sweating, drooling, and vomiting before becoming unresponsive. On examination, his clothes are damp with sweat and have a garlic-like odor. He is obtunded with labored breathing. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 48 (bradycardia), RR 12 (shallow, with audible secretions), BP 88/52, SpO2 84% on room air. Pupils are constricted bilaterally at 1 mm (miosis) and non-reactive. There are copious oral and bronchial secretions. Diffuse wheezing and crackles are auscultated. Fasciculations are visible in the extremities and face. He is incontinent of urine and stool. The patient is decontaminated, intubated for airway protection, and atropine 2 mg IV is administered with repeat dosing until secretions dry, followed by pralidoxime infusion.

Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

A 47-yr-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-wk history of a cough. She says the
cough is never productive, occurs at all times of the day (including at night), and is independent
of activity. She is not sure whether she had an upper respiratory tract infection preceding the
cough. She does recall that a new neighbor, who is a smoker, moved into a downstairs
apartment at the time the cough began. The neighbor frequently smokes outside the patient's
apartment window, triggering the cough.
She has not noticed any heartburn or runny nose. One month after the cough started, she
noticed pain at the right side of her breastbone occurring with stretching and deep breathing. At
that same time, she also noted that she has been wheezing during exertion. She has never had
wheezing before. She has had no shortness of breath.

A 48-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe retrosternal chest pain following an episode of forceful vomiting after a large meal with heavy alcohol consumption. The pain is constant, radiates to the back, and worsens with swallowing. He has vomited several more times since onset, and the last emesis contained streaks of blood. On examination, he appears acutely distressed, diaphoretic, and is splinting his chest. Vital signs: T 38.4C, HR 124, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 91%. Subcutaneous emphysema is palpable in the neck and anterior chest wall. Auscultation reveals a crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat over the precordium (Hamman sign) and decreased breath sounds at the left base. Chest X-ray reveals left-sided pleural effusion, pneumomediastinum, and subcutaneous emphysema. CT chest with oral contrast demonstrates extravasation of contrast from the distal esophagus into the left pleural space.

A 48-year-old overweight male mail carrier with a BMI of 31 presents with a 2-month history of sharp stabbing pain in the bottom of his right heel. The pain is most severe with the first few steps in the morning and after standing up from prolonged sitting, then gradually improves with activity but returns after extended periods of walking on his mail route. He walks approximately 8 miles daily on pavement. He wears standard-issue work boots without orthotic inserts. He denies any trauma, numbness, tingling, or night pain. On examination, there is exquisite point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle at the origin of the plantar fascia. Pain is reproduced with passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass test). Achilles tendon is nontender and intact. Heel fat pad is unremarkable. There is tightness of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex bilaterally. Neurovascular examination is intact. Weight-bearing lateral foot radiograph shows a small calcaneal spur, which is noted to be an incidental and common finding.

A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours per episode, occurring approximately twice monthly. Each episode is preceded by a sensation of fullness in her right ear and accompanied by roaring tinnitus and reduced hearing on the right side. Between episodes she notes persistent mild tinnitus and a sense that her right ear hearing has gradually deteriorated. She experiences nausea and sometimes vomiting during attacks. She denies headache, visual changes, or focal neurological symptoms. Audiometry demonstrates low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with normal hearing on the left. On examination between episodes, vital signs are normal. The Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Neurological exam is nonfocal.

A 48-year-old woman with a history of migraine headaches presents to the emergency room with altered mental status over the last several hours. She was found by her husband, earlier in the day, to be acutely disoriented and increasingly somnolent. On physical examination, she has scleral icterus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and asterixis. Preliminary laboratory studies are notable for a serum ALT of 6498 units/L, total bilirubin of 5.6 mg/dL, and INR of 6.8. Her husband reports that she has consistently been taking pain medications and started taking additional 500 mg acetaminophen pills several days ago for lower back pain. Further history reveals a medication list with multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations.

A 48-yr-old woman comes to the office because of a nasal-sounding voice. She has been
treated in the past for chronic sinusitis and asthma. A year ago, she had balloon rhinoplasty to
enlarge her sinuses. Today, she says that she first noticed the nasal-sounding voice a week
after surgery, but it has become more apparent over the last 3 mo.
Today, she says it feels as though air escapes through her nose while speaking, giving it a
nasal quality. Her voice is better in the morning and worse later in the day. She says she does
not have dysphagia but notes occasional nasal regurgitation of liquids but not food. She denies
diplopia, drooping eyelids, loss of smell or taste, and difficulty with balance or gait. She denies
having arm and leg weakness and numbness.

A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.

A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for a spreading rash around her mouth and nose that began 5 days ago. It started as a small red spot near her left nostril and has since developed into multiple crusty lesions. Several children at her daycare have had similar sores. She is otherwise well with no fever, sore throat, or decreased appetite. On examination, there are multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with two satellite lesions on the left cheek. The lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in size. There is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement. There is mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. She has no history of eczema or immunodeficiency.

A 50-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of worsening lower back pain radiating bilaterally to both legs, progressive bilateral leg weakness, and difficulty urinating since yesterday. He has a history of lumbar disc disease with two prior episodes of sciatica managed conservatively. On examination, he walks with a wide-based unsteady gait. Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological exam reveals decreased strength (3/5) in bilateral ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, diminished patellar and absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally, and decreased perianal sensation with reduced anal sphincter tone on rectal exam. Post-void residual bladder scan shows 650 mL of retained urine. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals a large L4-L5 central disc herniation with severe compression of the cauda equina nerve roots.

dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

A 54-year-old woman presents with a 4-hour history of severe occipital headache, blurred vision, and progressive confusion. She has a history of chronic hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3 but ran out of her medications two weeks ago. On examination, she is disoriented to time and place. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 102, RR 22, BP 238/142, SpO2 96%. Fundoscopic exam reveals bilateral papilledema, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots. Neurological exam shows bilateral lower extremity hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign bilaterally. Labs: creatinine 3.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.6), urinalysis with 3+ protein and RBC casts. CT head is negative for hemorrhage but shows subtle posterior white matter edema suggestive of PRES.

A 55-year-old male long-haul truck driver presents with sudden onset of severe perianal pain that began yesterday while straining during a bowel movement. The pain is constant, throbbing, and rated 8 out of 10, significantly worse with sitting and defecation. He reports a palpable lump at the anal verge. He has a long history of intermittent hemorrhoidal symptoms including minor bleeding and itching, which he has managed with over-the-counter preparations. His occupation requires prolonged sitting for 10 to 12 hours daily, and he has a low-fiber diet with poor fluid intake. He denies fever, purulent drainage, or changes in bowel habits. On examination, there is a tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule approximately 2 cm in diameter at the anal verge, consistent with a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. There is surrounding mild edema but no erythema suggesting infection. Digital rectal exam is deferred due to pain.

A 55-year-old male professional painter presents with a 4-month history of progressively worsening right shoulder pain. The pain is dull and aching, localized to the lateral deltoid region, and significantly worse when reaching overhead or behind his back. He reports difficulty sleeping on his right side. A 55-year-old man presents with 2 days of bilateral flank pain, initially intermittent but now constant, with associated nausea, vomiting, and markedly decreased urine output over the past 18 hours. His past medical history includes recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and gout. On examination, he appears uncomfortable and mildly diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 37.9C, HR 104, RR 20, BP 156/92, SpO2 97%. Bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness is present. Abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic fullness. Labs reveal BUN 68 mg/dL, creatinine 6.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.1), potassium 5.9 mEq/L. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. CT abdomen without contrast demonstrates bilateral ureteral calculi, 8 mm on the right at the ureterovesical junction and 10 mm on the left at the mid-ureter, with bilateral hydronephrosis.

A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.

A 56-year-old woman who is a long-time patient returns to the office for scheduled follow up of her type 2 diabetes and chronically elevated blood glucose. At her last visit 3 months ago, her HbA1C was 7.6%, where it had been for several visits. You recommended beginning treatment with insulin, which she refused because of her fear of needles. You then increased her dose of glimepiride from 4 mg to 8 mg once a day and advised her to more strictly follow her diet and exercise regimen, which she claims to be doing. Per office protocol, a fingerstick glucose test on arrival today shows glucose level of 221mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L) and hemoglobin A1C 8.1%; urine dipstick is normal.

He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine intermittently. On examination, he is writhing in pain and appears ashen. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.

Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. Pulses are diminished in the left upper extremity. Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.

A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C) presents after two episodes of large-volume hematemesis over the past hour, each estimated at 500 mL of bright red blood with clots. He also reports black tarry stools for the past 2 days. He has known esophageal varices documented on prior endoscopy and has been non-compliant with propranolol therapy. On examination, he is pale, confused, and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 36.2C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 78/42, SpO2 94%. Abdominal exam reveals ascites, splenomegaly, and caput medusae. Rectal exam shows melena. Labs: hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL (baseline 10.4), platelets 62,000/mcL, INR 2.4, BUN 58 mg/dL. Two large-bore IVs are placed and massive transfusion protocol is activated.

A 58-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling of her right foot. She recalls stepping on a nail while walking barefoot in her yard four days ago. She cleaned the wound at the time but did not seek medical attention. She reports low-grade fever and mild chills. On examination, vital signs are temperature 100.6°F, heart rate 84, blood pressure 142/88. The right foot shows a puncture wound on the plantar surface with surrounding erythema extending 6 cm, warmth, edema, and tenderness. There is no crepitus or fluctuance. Peripheral pulses are diminished bilaterally. Her last tetanus booster was over 10 years ago.

A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.

A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite using his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes at home. He has a history of moderate persistent asthma with two prior ICU admissions. He recently had an upper respiratory infection. On examination, he is sitting upright, using accessory muscles, and speaking in single words only. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 152, RR 42, BP 100/65, SpO2 87% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with minimal wheezing, suggesting severe air trapping. Peak flow is unobtainable due to patient fatigue. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg.

A 6-year-old boy with a medical history significant for mild persistent asthma is brought to the clinic by his mother with a history of a 5-day cough. His mother reports that the child's fever continues to be elevated despite acetaminophen therapy. He has missed school for the past 3 days and he has a classmate sick with pneumonia. The mother reports that the appetite is good for the child. His cough produced yellowish sputum at home. His vitals at the clinic are: respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, heart rate 80 beats/min, and temperature 101.6°F (38.7°C). He appears in no respiratory distress. His lung examination reveals bilateral rales and occasional wheeze. CXR reveals lobar infiltrates without pleural effusions.

A 60-year-old woman presents with 5 days of progressive shortness of breath following a confirmed influenza A infection. Despite oseltamivir initiated 3 days ago, her respiratory status has continued to deteriorate. She has a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 38). On examination, she is in marked respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.9C, HR 118, RR 34, BP 106/62, SpO2 82% on high-flow nasal cannula at 60L/min and FiO2 100%. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse bilateral crackles. Chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, but echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function with no evidence of volume overload. ABG: pH 7.22, pO2 58, pCO2 52, PaO2/FiO2 ratio 58. She is intubated for mechanical ventilation.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of a painful, burning, vesicular rash on the left side of her forehead extending to the tip of her nose. She initially experienced a prodrome of tingling and deep aching pain over the left forehead for 2 days before the rash appeared. She now reports left eye redness, tearing, photophobia, and a gritty foreign body sensation. She has a history of well-controlled hypertension and had chickenpox as a child. She has not received the herpes zoster vaccine. On examination, temperature is 99.4°F. There are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base distributed along the left V1 (ophthalmic) division of the trigeminal nerve, involving the forehead, upper eyelid, and the tip of the nose (positive Hutchinson sign). The left eye shows conjunctival injection, mild periorbital edema, and a mildly hazy cornea. Visual acuity is 20/40 on the left (baseline 20/25) and 20/25 on the right. Intraocular pressure is 14 mmHg bilaterally. The right side of the face is entirely clear.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline GFR 22) on maintenance hemodialysis presents after missing his last two dialysis sessions due to transportation issues. He reports 2 days of progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations. He has continued to eat his usual diet, including bananas and orange juice. On examination, he appears fatigued and mildly short of breath. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 52 (irregular), RR 20, BP 172/96, SpO2 95%. Lower extremity exam reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Labs: potassium 7.8 mEq/L, BUN 112 mg/dL, creatinine 11.4 mg/dL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, phosphorus 8.2 mg/dL. ECG demonstrates absent P waves, widened QRS complexes (duration 180 ms), and peaked T waves with a sine wave pattern beginning to emerge. IV calcium gluconate is administered emergently.

A 62-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis managed with daily naproxen for the past 3 years presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea. The pain is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating. She denies vomiting, hematemesis, melena, or unintentional weight loss. She does not smoke but drinks one glass of wine nightly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. A fecal occult blood test is negative. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.

A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.

A 65-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer (Gleason 9, diagnosed 2 years ago) presents with 10 days of progressive mid-back pain and 4 days of increasing difficulty walking. He now requires a walker. He also reports a band-like sensation around his trunk at the level of the umbilicus and difficulty initiating urination. On examination, he appears cachectic. Vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals increased tone and spasticity in both lower extremities, bilateral lower extremity weakness (3/5 hip flexors, 4/5 knee extensors), hyperreflexia with bilateral ankle clonus, upgoing plantar responses (positive Babinski bilaterally), and a sensory level at approximately T10. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrates a large epidural mass at T9-T10 causing significant spinal cord compression with cord signal changes.

A 65-year-old man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of a productive cough and fever. He has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F), a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92 percent while breathing room air. Physical examination reveals only crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field. The white-cell count is 14,000 per cubic millimeter, and the results of routine chemical tests are normal. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe.

A 65-year-old woman presents with recurring episodes of painful cramping in her right calf that wake her from sleep, occurring 2 to 3 times per week for the past month. Each episode lasts a few minutes and resolves with stretching or walking. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for mild hypertension. She denies leg swelling, skin color changes, or daytime calf pain. On examination, vital signs are normal. Both calves are non-tender, symmetric in size, and without edema. Peripheral pulses are intact bilaterally. There is no varicosity, skin discoloration, or warmth. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is unremarkable.

She had been recuperating at home but on beginning to mobilize and walk, the right leg became painful, tender, and swollen. On examination, the right calf is 4 cm greater in circumference than the left when measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Superficial veins in the leg are more dilated on the right foot and the right leg is slightly redder than the left. There is some tenderness on palpation in the popliteal fossa behind the knee.

On examination, the right calf is 4 cm greater in circumference than the left when measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Superficial veins in the leg are more dilated on the right foot and the right leg is slightly redder than the left. There is some tenderness on palpation in the popliteal fossa behind the knee.

A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.

The patient has a 100-pack-year history of smoking. She has had intermittent, low-grade fever of 100°F (37.7°C) for the past 3 days and her appetite is poor. She has required increased use of rescue bronchodilator therapy in addition to her maintenance medications to control symptoms.

A 68-year-old male farmer presents with a slowly growing lesion on his nose that he first noticed approximately 8 months ago. The lesion has gradually enlarged and occasionally bleeds when he washes his face but heals over. He has extensive sun exposure from decades of outdoor work and a history of multiple sunburns in his youth. He has never had skin cancer before. On examination, there is a 1.2 cm pearly, dome-shaped nodule on the left ala of the nose with a rolled border and central depression. Multiple telangiectasias are visible on the surface. The surrounding skin shows significant solar damage with actinic keratoses on the forehead and ears. There is no palpable cervical or preauricular lymphadenopathy. A dermoscopic examination reveals arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests.

A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.

A 68-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure comes to the office because of a
1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a
flight of stairs without stopping. Now he must stop every few steps to rest because of dyspnea
but not chest discomfort. He also complains of lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea,
cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies
chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope or near syncope. He has had no fever or upper
respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes managed with glipizide and metformin is found confused and diaphoretic on his living room floor by his daughter. She reports he has had poor oral intake for the past 2 days due to a gastrointestinal illness with vomiting and diarrhea but continued taking all medications. On examination by EMS, he is obtunded, drenched in sweat, and exhibiting intermittent tremors. Vital signs: T 35.8C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 162/94, SpO2 96%. Finger-stick glucose reads 28 mg/dL. Neurological exam shows bilateral extensor plantar responses, generalized hyperreflexia, and no focal deficits. EMS administers 25 g of dextrose 50% IV with improvement in mental status within minutes, but glucose subsequently drops again to 42 mg/dL, requiring a continuous dextrose 10% infusion.

A 68-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for the past 12 years presents with a 4-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, and difficulty with balance. She reports her tongue has been sore intermittently. She has noticed increased forgetfulness and mild cognitive slowing. She takes no supplements. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears pale with a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis). Neurological examination reveals diminished vibration and proprioception in both feet and ankles, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Gait is wide-based and mildly ataxic. Upper extremity neurological exam is normal. CBC reveals hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Peripheral blood smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 level is critically low at 85 pg/mL (normal 200-900). Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels are both elevated.

They have noticed increased drooling and that she constantly chews on her fingers and toys. She is eating slightly less than usual but still taking adequate formula. She has no fever, no diarrhea, and no rash. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The infant is mildly irritable but consolable. The lower gingiva is mildly swollen and erythematous over the area of the central incisors, and a tooth bud is palpable beneath the surface. The remainder of the exam is normal.

A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.

A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.

A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant. He reports decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a total knee replacement. On examination, he is afebrile at 37.2C but appears mildly uncomfortable. Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 134/78, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. WBC is only mildly elevated at 11,200/mcL. CT abdomen with contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection suggestive of early perforation.

A 72-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics presents with 2 days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake. His wife reports he has been increasingly lethargic and today was unable to recognize her. On examination, he is obtunded, with warm, flushed skin. Vital signs: T 39.4C, HR 122, RR 26, BP 76/44 (MAP 55), SpO2 93% on room air. Suprapubic tenderness is present with a distended bladder. Foley catheter insertion yields 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine. Labs: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.2), lactate 5.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, platelets 82,000/mcL. Urinalysis shows too numerous to count WBC and bacteria. SOFA score is 11. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are initiated.

A 72-year-old woman presents with generalized dry, itchy skin that has been worsening over the past several weeks as winter has progressed. She reports the itching is worst on her shins and forearms. She bathes daily in hot water and uses regular bar soap. She denies any new medications, rash, jaundice, or unintentional weight loss. On examination, the skin on the extremities is diffusely dry with fine scaling and superficial cracking. There are no excoriations, erythematous plaques, or papules. Skin turgor is appropriate for age. No jaundice or lymphadenopathy is noted.

A 74-yr-old man comes to the Emergency Department (ED) because of a several-month history of increasing exertional chest pain. He states that after walking a few feet he feels left-sided chest pressure that radiates down his left arm. Lately, the pain has been associated with dyspnea and nausea. The pain is relieved by rest within a few minutes. He saw his primary care physician a few days ago. At that time, he was given a prescription for sublingual nitroglycerin as a therapeutic trial and was scheduled for an outpatient stress test in a few weeks. He comes to the ED today because the episodes have been occurring more frequently and with less exertion. He says today that when he takes the sublingual nitroglycerin, it does relieve his symptoms.

A 74-yr-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of an
episode of confusion. The day prior to her visit she attended a wedding at which she had "2 or
3" glasses of wine and afterwards felt extremely tired whereby she left early. When she got
home, she went straight to bed without even undressing. She awoke about 3 h later and didn't

A 75-year-old woman presents with severe, diffuse abdominal pain of sudden onset 4 hours ago. She describes the pain as 10/10, constant, and poorly localized. Her past medical history includes atrial fibrillation (on apixaban), congestive heart failure, and hypertension. She recently self-discontinued her anticoagulation. On examination, she appears acutely distressed and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 37.6C, HR 112 (irregularly irregular), RR 24, BP 102/64, SpO2 95%. Remarkably, abdominal examination reveals only mild diffuse tenderness with no guarding or rebound despite her severe pain level. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Labs: WBC 18,400/mcL, lactate 6.2 mmol/L, LDH 520 U/L. CT angiography of the abdomen reveals a filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery consistent with acute embolus.

A 78-year-old man is brought in after a syncopal episode at home witnessed by his wife. She reports he has been increasingly fatigued and lightheaded for the past week. His past medical history includes aortic stenosis, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he is alert but pale and mildly confused. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 32, RR 18, BP 82/50, SpO2 93%. Cannon A waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. Heart sounds reveal a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border and variable intensity of S1. ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular escape rate of 32 bpm, wide QRS complexes, and independent P waves at a rate of 82 bpm.

A 9-month-old male infant is brought in by his parents after 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs up to his abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy. The parents report two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material. He had a viral upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, during a pain-free interval, the infant is pale and lethargic. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 168, RR 36, BP 80/52. Abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. The right lower quadrant feels empty (Dance sign). Rectal exam reveals currant jelly stool on the examining finger. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant, confirming ileocolic intussusception, with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Air enema reduction is arranged.

A family of four, including a 42-year-old father, 39-year-old mother, 14-year-old daughter, and 10-year-old son, present to the emergency department in January with similar symptoms of severe headache, nausea, dizziness, and confusion. The father reports their home gas furnace has been making unusual noises and he noticed a strange smell over the past week. The mother and daughter are vomiting. The son is the most severely affected, exhibiting marked confusion and difficulty walking. On examination of the father: Vital signs T 37.0C, HR 104, RR 22, BP 148/88, SpO2 reading 98% (unreliable with CO). His skin has a cherry-red hue. He is oriented to person only. The son is obtunded with GCS 10. Venous carboxyhemoglobin levels return: father 32%, mother 28%, daughter 26%, son 38%. The family is placed on 100% non-rebreather masks and transfer is arranged to a facility with hyperbaric oxygen capability. The fire department is dispatched to the home.

An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with 4 days of profuse watery diarrhea (10-12 episodes daily) and vomiting (6-8 episodes daily). They report he has been increasingly listless and has had no wet diapers in the past 10 hours. He recently started daycare and several children there have been ill with gastroenteritis. On examination, the infant is limp and lethargic with a weak, barely audible cry. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 182, RR 32, BP 68/38 (hypotensive for age), capillary refill 5 seconds. Weight is 9.8 kg (previous weight at well-child visit 2 weeks ago was 11.2 kg, representing a 12.5% weight loss). Labs: sodium 158 mEq/L, potassium 2.8 mEq/L, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (elevated for age), bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, glucose 62 mg/dL. IV normal saline bolus 20 mL/kg is initiated.

An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove onto himself approximately 45 minutes ago. He sustained scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of his face. He has been crying inconsolably. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is alert but in severe pain and distress. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 152, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 98%. Weight is 28 kg. Burns cover approximately 20% total body surface area: areas of erythema with large intact and ruptured blisters (superficial partial thickness) on the chest and abdomen, with waxy white insensate areas (deep partial to full thickness) on both forearms. No circumferential burns are identified. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs and no evidence of inhalation injury. He has no hoarseness or stridor. Parkland formula is calculated (20% TBSA x 28 kg x 4 mL = 2,240 mL LR over first 24 hours), IV access is obtained, and morphine is administered for pain.

An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Her mother reports that her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching. On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. A mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping examined under microscopy reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets.

On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. A mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping examined under microscopy reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets.

An 80-yr-old woman is brought to the emergency department by emergency medical services
(EMS) personnel because of a syncopal episode at home. She had been in the shower,
suddenly felt weak, and collapsed to the floor. Her husband heard her fall and found her awake,
lying on the bathroom floor. He called EMS who, when they arrived in the patient's home,
found her to be tachycardic and hypotensive. On arrival in the emergency department, she is
confused and has difficulty answering questions. Her husband states she has hypertension,
dyslipidemia, and mild dementia and, 1 wk ago, had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement for
severe aortic stenosis. He was told the procedure had been uncomplicated and states that his
wife had been feeling well during her recovery. She has never had an event like this one before.
